questions.stem: The basic economic problem of relative scarcity exists because:
options: governments restrict the amount of resources firms may use
prices rise whenever demand for a product increases quickly
wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited
some resources, such as gold, are rare compared with other resources
questions.explanation: Scarcity is relative: resources are limited compared with the wants people have for them. Even common resources are scarce in this sense, so every society must make choices.

questions.stem: Opportunity cost is:
options: the total money price that is paid for a good or service when it is bought
the value of all the alternatives given up when a choice is made
the extra profit a business earns by choosing the cheapest option
the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the single most valued alternative forgone, not every option rejected. It applies whether or not money changes hands.

questions.stem: A city council can spend $50 million on either a new bikeway or a new library. It builds the bikeway. The opportunity cost of this decision is:
options: the library, the alternative the council gave up
the $50 million the council spent on building the bikeway
the bikeway, the project the council chose
the cost of maintaining the bikeway each year
questions.explanation: With limited funds, choosing the bikeway means forgoing the library, its next best use. The dollar outlay measures the money spent, but the true cost is what else those resources could have provided.

questions.stem: Two students face the same choice between a paid shift and a study session, but one works and the other studies. In economic terms this is best explained by the fact that:
options: opportunity cost applies only to choices that involve spending money
the student who works faces no opportunity cost from the choice
each student values the benefits and costs of the options differently
one of the two students has failed to consider the opportunity cost
questions.explanation: Benefits are measured subjectively against costs, so people facing the same options can rationally choose differently. Both students still face an opportunity cost, whichever option they choose.

questions.stem: Which statement about the basic economic problem is correct?
options: Wealthy countries have solved scarcity, so they no longer face choices
Scarcity applies to goods but not to services such as health and education
Individuals, businesses and governments at every level must make choices
Only governments face scarcity, as households can borrow to buy what they want
questions.explanation: Scarcity forces choices on everyone, from households and local councils to national governments. Even rich countries must choose how to use limited resources.

questions.stem: The income earned by the factor of production capital is:
options: profit
interest
rent
wages
questions.explanation: Each factor earns a matching income: land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurial ability earns profit.

questions.stem: A Queensland sugar cane farm uses farmland, cane harvesters, seasonal workers and an owner who organises the business and bears its risks. The owner's contribution is:
options: capital, which earns interest on the farm's equipment
labour, which earns wages for managing the farm
land, which earns rent from the farm's paddocks
entrepreneurial ability, which earns profit
questions.explanation: Organising the other factors and taking the risk of loss is entrepreneurial ability, rewarded by profit. The harvesters are capital and the farmland is land.

questions.stem: As a factor of production, 'land' includes:
options: machinery and buildings used to produce other goods
the money that firms borrow to buy their equipment
all natural resources, such as minerals, forests and water
only the area of ground on which factories and offices are built
questions.explanation: Economists use land for every gift of nature used in production, including minerals, fish stocks and water. Machinery and buildings are capital, and money is not itself a factor of production.

questions.stem: The ceteris paribus assumption means:
options: every economic variable changes at exactly the same rate over time
buyers and sellers always act in their own self-interest
the economy is always operating at full employment
other things being equal, with all other factors held constant
questions.explanation: Ceteris paribus lets economists isolate the effect of one change by assuming nothing else changes. Without it, the cause of an observed effect would be unclear.

questions.stem: Economists use simplified models, such as the production possibility curve, mainly because:
options: models describe every feature of the real economy with complete accuracy
simple models always predict future events without any error
real economies are too small to be studied without a model
assumptions remove detail so that key relationships can be identified
questions.explanation: Models leave out complicating detail, through assumptions, so that the relationship being studied stands out. They are useful even though they are not complete descriptions of reality.

questions.stem: The production possibility curve (frontier) shows:
options: the combinations of two goods that consumers in the economy would most prefer to buy
the prices at which producers are willing to supply two goods to the market
the amounts of two goods an economy imports and exports in a given year
the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all resources fully used
questions.explanation: The curve assumes a fixed quantity of resources and given technology, fully and efficiently employed. Points on it are the most that can be produced; it says nothing about prices or preferences.

questions.stem: Which is one of the assumptions used when drawing a production possibility curve?
options: The quantity of resources and the state of technology are fixed
The economy produces an unlimited number of different goods
Resources are equally suited to producing every good
The prices of the two goods are always equal
questions.explanation: Holding resources and technology constant lets the curve show the trade-off at a point in time. A bowed curve actually reflects resources that are not equally suited to both goods.

questions.stem: An economy is producing at a point inside its production possibility curve. This shows that:
options: the economy has achieved allocative efficiency
the economy has experienced economic growth
some resources are unemployed or underutilised
the economy is producing beyond its capacity
questions.explanation: Inside the curve, more of one or both goods could be made without giving anything up, so resources are idle or used inefficiently. Points beyond the curve are unattainable with current resources.

questions.stem: A point lying outside an economy's production possibility curve represents a combination of goods that:
options: can be produced only if some of its resources are left unemployed
is produced when the economy is in a recession
is produced most efficiently by the economy now
cannot be produced with the economy's current resources and technology
questions.explanation: The curve marks the limit of current productive capacity. Reaching a point outside it requires economic growth, such as more resources or better technology.

questions.stem: An economy on its production possibility curve decides to produce more health services. It must produce fewer other goods. This illustrates:
options: a trade-off, with the forgone goods as the opportunity cost
economic growth, as the economy now produces more output
underutilisation of resources in the health sector
a shift of the curve caused by new technology
questions.explanation: On the curve all resources are in use, so more of one good requires moving resources away from others. The goods given up are the opportunity cost of the extra health services.

questions.stem: An economy's production possibilities are (capital goods, consumer goods): (0, 100), (10, 90), (20, 70), (30, 40), (40, 0). Moving from 20 to 30 capital goods, what is the opportunity cost of each extra capital good?
options: 30 consumer goods
2 consumer goods
4 consumer goods
3 consumer goods
questions.explanation: Consumer goods fall from 70 to 40, a loss of 30, for 10 more capital goods, so each capital good costs 30 / 10 = 3 consumer goods. The total of 30 is the cost of all ten units, not of each one.

questions.stem: For the production possibilities (capital goods, consumer goods): (0, 100), (10, 90), (20, 70), (30, 40), (40, 0), the opportunity cost of each extra 10 capital goods keeps rising. This is because:
options: the government taxes the production of capital goods more heavily
resources are not equally suited to producing both types of good
the economy has more resources than it can use in production
consumers prefer capital goods to consumer goods as incomes rise
questions.explanation: As production of capital goods expands, resources better suited to consumer goods must be shifted, so more consumer goods are given up for each extra unit. This is why the curve bows outwards.

questions.stem: On a production possibility curve diagram, economic growth is shown by:
options: an inward shift of the whole curve
an outward shift of the whole curve
a movement along the curve
a movement to a point inside the curve
questions.explanation: Growth means the economy can produce more of both goods, so its whole frontier moves out. A movement along the curve only changes the mix of output.

questions.stem: Which event is most likely to shift a country's production possibility curve outwards?
options: Improvements in health and education that raise labour productivity
A recession that leaves many workers without jobs for a time
A decision to produce more consumer goods and fewer capital goods
A rise in the prices of goods the economy produces
questions.explanation: Healthier, better-educated workers can produce more, raising productive capacity. A recession moves the economy inside the curve without shifting it.

questions.stem: A new technology greatly raises output in agriculture but has no effect on manufacturing. On a production possibility curve with agricultural goods on one axis and manufactured goods on the other, the curve will:
options: shift inwards along the agricultural goods axis
pivot outwards along the agricultural goods axis only
shift outwards equally along both axes
pivot outwards along the manufactured goods axis only
questions.explanation: An asymmetric technology advance raises the maximum output of agriculture, while maximum manufacturing output is unchanged, so the curve pivots out from the manufacturing intercept. The economy can still gain more of both goods by reallocating resources.

questions.stem: A war destroys a large share of a country's factories, roads and power stations. On its production possibility curve, this is shown as:
options: an outward shift of the curve
a movement along the curve
a movement to a point outside the curve
an inward shift of the curve
questions.explanation: Losing capital reduces the economy's maximum possible output, so the frontier moves inwards. A famine that reduces the labour force has a similar effect.

questions.stem: During a recession unemployment rises, but no resources are destroyed and technology is unchanged. On the production possibility curve, the economy:
options: stays on the curve, but the curve shifts inwards
moves from a point inside the curve to a point on it
moves along the curve towards more capital goods
moves from a point on the curve to a point inside it
questions.explanation: The economy's capacity is unchanged, so the curve does not move. Idle workers mean actual output falls below capacity, which is a point inside the curve.

questions.stem: Country X devotes a larger share of its resources to capital goods today than Country Y does, with both starting on similar production possibility curves. In the future, Country X is likely to:
options: see its curve shift inwards, as consumer goods are given up today
have the same future curve, as today's choices do not affect capacity
produce outside its curve today without any opportunity cost
see its curve shift out faster, at the cost of fewer consumer goods now
questions.explanation: Capital goods such as machinery raise future productive capacity, so X's frontier grows faster. The opportunity cost is fewer consumer goods, and lower current living standards, today.

questions.stem: The three basic economic questions every economy must answer are:
options: what and how much to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce
where to produce, when to produce, and why to produce
what to import, what to export, and what to tax
how much to save, how much to spend, and how much money to borrow
questions.explanation: Because resources are scarce, every economy must decide the output mix, the production methods and the distribution of output. Different economic systems answer these questions in different ways.

questions.stem: A manufacturer decides whether to replace assembly-line workers with robots. This decision addresses which basic economic question?
options: What to produce
For whom to produce
How much to produce
How to produce
questions.explanation: Choosing between labour and capital is a decision about the method of production. The product being made has not changed.

questions.stem: The government increases the age pension, funded by higher taxes on high-income earners. Which basic economic question is it mainly answering?
options: For whom to produce
How to produce
What to produce
Where to produce
questions.explanation: Transfer payments change who has the income to buy goods and services, so they alter the distribution of output. That is the 'for whom' question.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes efficiency from equity?
options: Efficiency and equity both mean producing the maximum output from given resources
Efficiency applies only to businesses, while equity applies only to governments
Efficiency is about how well resources are used; equity is about how fairly they and incomes are shared
Efficiency is about how fairly incomes are shared; equity is about how well resources are used
questions.explanation: Efficiency concerns getting the most from scarce resources. Equity concerns fairness in who owns resources and receives output, which is a value judgement as well as an economic question.

questions.stem: A government raises taxes on high incomes to fund larger payments to low-income households. Critics argue this may reduce incentives to work and invest. This illustrates:
options: a movement outside the production possibility curve
a change in how to produce, not for whom to produce
a possible trade-off between equity and efficiency
an improvement in both equity and efficiency
questions.explanation: Redistribution can make incomes fairer but may weaken incentives, which could reduce output. Governments must weigh the two goals against each other.

questions.stem: In a market economy, the three basic economic questions are answered mainly by:
options: custom and tradition passed down through earlier generations
elected governments voting on the production of every good
consumers and businesses interacting through the price mechanism
a central planning authority that sets output targets for each firm
questions.explanation: In a market system, private owners of resources respond to prices, which signal what consumers want and what is profitable to produce. Central planning answers the questions through government directives.

questions.stem: Which country is the clearest example of a centrally planned (command) economy?
options: North Korea
Singapore
United States
Norway
questions.explanation: In North Korea the state owns most resources and decides what is produced, how and for whom. Singapore, the United States and Norway are market-based economies with differing degrees of government involvement.

questions.stem: The United Kingdom provides most health care free of charge through the government's National Health Service, while private firms produce most other goods and services. This makes the United Kingdom:
options: a traditional economy
a pure market economy
a mixed economy
a command economy
questions.explanation: Most resources are allocated by markets, but government provides major services such as health care and regulates markets. That combination defines a mixed economy, as in Australia.

questions.stem: Compared with the United Kingdom, the United States relies more on private insurance and private providers to deliver health care. This means that in the United States:
options: health care is allocated mainly by custom and tradition
the market plays a larger role in deciding who receives health care
the government decides who receives all health care through planning
health care is not affected by the basic economic problem at all
questions.explanation: When care is bought through private insurance, ability to pay plays a larger part in answering 'for whom'. Public programs exist, but the government's role is smaller than in the UK system.

questions.stem: Norway saves much of its government oil revenue in a large sovereign wealth fund and funds extensive public services, while most goods are produced by private firms. This shows that Norway is:
options: a traditional economy in which custom decides how resources are used
a mixed market economy in which government plays a large role in 'for whom'
a command economy in which the state plans the output of every single industry
a pure market economy in which government plays no economic role
questions.explanation: Norway relies on markets for most production, but the state manages oil wealth and provides generous services, strongly shaping the distribution of income. It is a market economy with a large government role.

questions.stem: Singapore is open to trade and investment and relies on markets for most production, but the government provides most housing and holds stakes in major companies. Singapore is best described as:
options: a market economy with significant government involvement
a centrally planned economy with no private businesses
a traditional economy based on custom and inherited roles
a pure market economy in which the state owns no assets
questions.explanation: Singapore combines free markets and openness with a strong state presence through public housing and government-linked companies. It shows that market economies differ widely in the role of government.

questions.stem: Since reforms that began in 1978, China's economy has moved:
options: from a market economy towards strict central planning of all production and prices
from a mixed economy towards a traditional economy based on custom
from state ownership to complete private ownership of every industry
from central planning towards markets, with large state-owned enterprises remaining
questions.explanation: China allowed private enterprise, foreign investment and market prices to play a growing role, describing the result as a 'socialist market economy'. The state still owns major enterprises and directs key sectors.

questions.stem: In Cuba, most major decisions about what and how to produce have been made by:
options: local communities following custom and inherited traditions
the state through central planning, with limited private enterprise
private firms responding to prices, with limited state involvement
foreign multinational corporations operating under free trade rules
questions.explanation: Cuba's economy is dominated by state ownership and planning, although private small businesses have been permitted in limited areas. It sits towards the command end of the spectrum.

questions.stem: A common weakness of centrally planned economies is that:
options: markets produce far too many public goods because firms can easily charge everyone who benefits
income is always distributed very unequally because the state owns no property
consumers have too much choice, so firms produce too many varieties of each good
without price signals and profit incentives, shortages, surpluses and slow innovation are common
questions.explanation: Planners lack the information prices provide about what consumers want, and workers and managers have weaker incentives to cut costs or innovate. Market economies face different problems, such as under-providing public goods.

questions.stem: A strength of market economies is their responsiveness to consumers, but a common weakness is that:
options: they can produce large income inequality and under-provide public goods
they cannot respond to changes in consumer preferences without planners
they always produce less output than centrally planned economies
they leave resources such as labour permanently unemployed
questions.explanation: Markets distribute output according to income and wealth, which can be very unequal, and they fail to provide goods people can use without paying. These weaknesses are why most economies are mixed.
